paper_context.research_question: Can large-scale training data for event extraction be generated automatically by combining world knowledge (Freebase) and linguistic knowledge (FrameNet) with a soft distant supervision pipeline, and is the automatically labeled data of sufficient quality to train event extraction models and to augment human-annotated datasets?
main_claims: A pipeline that detects key arguments from Freebase, finds and expands triggers using FrameNet, and applies a Soft Distant Supervision (SDS) assumption can automatically generate large-scale labeled event extraction data from Wikipedia.

The automatically generated dataset (72k+ labeled sentences for 21 event types; 421k sentences using key-arguments-only) attains high precision under manual inspection (trigger labeling ~88.9%, argument labeling ~85.4%).

Models trained on the automatically labeled data perform competitively with models trained on human-annotated ACE data, and combining the automatic data with ACE training data improves event extraction performance on ACE test sets.
Proposed ranking metrics (Key Rate for arguments, Trigger Rate for verbs) and the use of FrameNet for trigger filtering/expansion are effective components in producing useful labels.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Precision of automatically labeled triggers and arguments (manual annotation of sampled sentences)
Extrinsic utility: downstream event extraction performance when training models on automatic data alone and combined with human-annotated ACE (P/R/F on ACE test set)
Ablation/analysis of key components (KR vs RS/ER; TR vs TCF/TETF; effect of FrameNet expansion)
Scale and coverage: number of event instances/sentences generated per Freebase event type and mapping coverage to ACE event types
Robustness to noisy labels: effectiveness of multi-instance learning (DMCNN-MIL) for mitigating distant supervision noise (held-out and manual evaluation of extracted events)
Reproducibility and resource utility: availability and clarity of released labeled dataset and mapping to KB/event types

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: A sentence that mentions all chosen key arguments of a Freebase CVT instance and contains a mapped trigger word likely expresses the corresponding event (Soft Distant Supervision assumption).

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If sentences containing all key arguments + trigger do not actually express the event (e.g., mentions are incidental or arguments refer to different events), generated labels will be noisy, degrading both manual precision and downstream model performance; MIL may not fully mitigate systematic noise.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Key Rate (KR = RS * ER) computed from Freebase counts identifies arguments that are both salient within an event type and discriminative across event types, and top-K by KR are sufficient to find event mentions in text.

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If KR ranks non-salient or non-mentionable arguments highly (e.g., arguments that are rarely expressed in text or are ambiguous), then the labeled data will miss many event instances or include false positives; choice of K (top-K) affects recall/precision tradeoff.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Mapping Freebase event type names to FrameNet frames via average word embeddings of type names and lexical units yields correct frame alignments useful for filtering noisy verbal triggers and expanding nominal triggers.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: §3.3 Trigger Word Filtering and Expansion; Equation 7

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Freebase CVTs and Wikipedia article mentions are sufficiently aligned (entity linking / matching) so that detecting mentions of Freebase argument values in Wikipedia sentences is reliable using CoreNLP NER and string matching.

Reliability of FrameNet mapping via word embeddings for trigger filtering and expansion (§3.3).
Quality and representativeness of the automatically labeled dataset (scale, per-type distribution, and manual precision sampling methodology) (§5.1-5.2).

chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should first validate low-level operations: (1) reproduce entity matching from Freebase CVT values to Wikipedia sentence mentions using the same NER and matching heuristics, (2) recompute KR and TR values from the same Freebase/Wikipedia snapshots to verify candidate selection and dataset sizes.

Then test component claims independently: (a) evaluate KR vs RS/ER for key-argument selection by measuring how often top-K arguments are mentioned in Wikipedia sentences; (b) evaluate TR and FrameNet mapping by measuring precision/recall of trigger lexicons against gold triggers (if available) or manual annotations.

Next, evaluate SDS labeling quality by sampling generated labels stratified by event type and by (i) presence of all key arguments but no trigger, (ii) presence of key arguments + trigger from initial TR lexicon, and (iii) presence after FrameNet expansion—this helps isolate which stages contribute most to label noise.

For extrinsic evaluation, verify that Wikipedia documents used for labeling are disjoint from ACE test documents to avoid data leakage; recompute ACE experiments with significance tests and per-type breakdowns.
For MIL and model claims, replicate DMCNN-MIL training with controlled noise/noise-free datasets to quantify robustness and bound expected performance gains from MIL.

Where evidence is incomplete (e.g., mapping/threshold choices), downstream reviewers should request or reconstruct exact preprocessing scripts, mapping tables, and hyperparameter selection logs to ensure reproducibility.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a pipeline to automatically generate large-scale event extraction training data by combining Freebase (world knowledge) and FrameNet (linguistic knowledge). Core algorithmic elements are: Key Rate (KR) for selecting a small set of key arguments per Freebase CVT, Trigger Rate (TR) computed from candidate verbs in sentences containing key arguments, embedding-based mapping from Freebase event type names to FrameNet frames for trigger filtering/nominal expansion, and a Soft Distant Supervision (SDS) labeling rule that marks sentences containing all key arguments plus a trigger as expressing the event. The generated dataset (421k KA-only, 72k KA+T) is evaluated via (i) manual precision on a 500-sample annotation, (ii) extrinsic ACE experiments where ED augments or replaces ACE training data, (iii) ablations over KR/RS/ER and TR/TCF/TETF/FrameNet, and (iv) held-out and manual evaluations for a DMCNN-MIL extractor trained on the noisy data. The paper chains these components to argue that automatically generated labels are of high enough quality to train and augment supervised extractors. The logical chain is mostly coherent: low-level heuristics (KR/TR/FrameNet mapping) feed labeled instances, SDS creates noisy labels, and MIL/DMCNN is used to mitigate noise. Gaps include sensitivity analyses (hyperparameter sensitivity, per-type precision/recall, mapping correctness), annotator bias risk, potential data-leakage checks, and limited statistical reporting (CIs, significance). Overall, the argument is plausible and partially supported by experiments, but relies on several heuristic mappings and operational choices whose robustness/generalizability are not fully established.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Problem statement — supervised EE is limited by scarce human-labeled data and narrow event type coverage (ACE statistics).
P2: Opportunity — Freebase contains many CVTs (event-like CVTs) and Wikipedia provides large text to potentially ground them.
P3: Challenge — event triggers are not present in KBs; matching full argument sets to single sentences is rare.

P4: Solution overview — choose representative 'key arguments' per CVT (KR) so that sentences are more likely to contain them; find trigger verbs in those sentences (TR); filter/expand triggers with FrameNet via embedding-based frame mapping; apply SDS to label sentences with key arguments + trigger as expressing the event.
P5: Implementation details — formal definitions of RS, ER, KR (Eqns 1-3); TCF, TETF, TR (Eqns 4-6); frame mapping via average word embeddings (Eqn 7); SDS labeling rule (§3.4).
P6: Dataset generation — apply the pipeline to 21 selected Freebase CVTs to yield 421k KA-only and 72k KA+T sentences (Table 2) using hyperparameters K=2 and TR=0.8.
P7: Intrinsic quality claim — manual annotation of 500 sampled labeled sentences yields ~88.9% trigger precision and ~85.4% argument precision (Table 3).
P8: Extrinsic utility claim — adding the generated data to ACE training (ACE+ED) improves DMCNN event extraction F1 on ACE test compared to ACE-only; ED-only is competitive (Table 4).
P9: Component-level claim — KR and TR metrics and FrameNet expansion provide measurable improvements in ACE experiments compared to ablations (Tables 5 and 6).
P10: Noise mitigation — DMCNN-MIL reduces DS noise as shown by held-out P-R curves and manual top-n precision (Figures 7-8, Table 7).

C: Conclusion — the SDS+KR+TR+FrameNet pipeline can produce large-scale labeled data of practical quality useful to train and augment EE systems, though robustness and some methodological choices need further validation.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents an SDS pipeline to generate large-scale event-extraction training data by combining Freebase CVTs (world knowledge) and FrameNet (linguistic knowledge). Components: Key Argument detection (KR = RS * ER) to pick top-K arguments; Trigger candidate ranking (TR = TCF * TETF) on verbs; FrameNet mapping via averaged word embeddings to filter verbal triggers and expand nominal triggers; SDS labeling rule that a sentence containing all key arguments + mapped trigger expresses the event. Generated dataset sizes: ~421k sentences using key-arguments-only (KA) and ~72.6k using KA+triggers (KA+T) across 21 Freebase types. Manual sampling (500 examples, 3 annotators including authors/colleagues) reports trigger precision 88.9% and argument precision 85.4%. Extrinsic evaluation: training DMCNN (and DMCNN-MIL) on ED-only and ACE+ED shows improvements over ACE-only baselines on ACE test. Ablations show KR and TR (with FrameNet) give small gains. MIL helps against DS noise (held-out P-R and manual top-n evaluation). Key methodological assumptions include validity of SDS (presence of key args + trigger implies event), correctness of embedding-based FrameNet mapping, reliability of entity matching from Freebase to Wikipedia, and manual mapping to ACE for extrinsic evaluation. The results are plausible but depend on multiple heuristic choices (K=2, TR threshold=0.8) and evaluation choices (small manual sample with non-independent annotators, held-out evaluation using incomplete Freebase). Missing or under-specified elements hamper reproducibility and robustness assessment: exact preprocessing/matching scripts, mapping tables (Freebase->FrameNet, Freebase->ACE), per-event-type precision/recall and sampling variance, statistics on overlap between Wikipedia and ACE test documents, and sensitivity analyses for hyperparameters and embedding choices.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes an engineering pipeline to automatically generate large-scale event extraction training data by combining world knowledge (Freebase CVTs) with linguistic knowledge (FrameNet) and a Soft Distant Supervision (SDS) labeling rule. Core algorithmic pieces are: Key Rate (KR = RoleSaliency * EventRelevance) to pick top-K key arguments per event type; Trigger Rate (TR = TCF * TETF) to rank verbal trigger candidates from sentences containing those key arguments; an embedding-based mapping from Freebase event type names to FrameNet frames to filter/expand trigger lexica (nominal triggers); and an SDS labeling assumption that sentences containing all key arguments plus a mapped trigger likely express the event. The authors release a dataset (421k KA-only; 72k KA+trigger) for 21 Freebase CVTs, report manual precision estimates (~88.9% triggers, ~85.4% arguments on a 500-sample annotation), and show extrinsic gains when combining the automatic data with ACE training (ACE+ED improves DMCNN F1 relative to ACE-only). Multi-instance learning (DMCNN-MIL) is applied to mitigate distant-supervision noise and is claimed to help in held-out and manual evaluations. Overall, the work applies and combines known DS ideas with targeted heuristics (KR/TR) and FrameNet filtering to produce a usable resource; the contribution is mostly incremental but practically useful if reproducible.
logical_argument_graph: Freebase CVTs encode multi-argument event instances but lack triggers in text → need to infer triggers and locate mentions in text to label sentences.

Not all arguments are equally useful for locating mentions → define Role Saliency (RS) and Event Relevance (ER) → combine to Key Rate (KR) to pick top-K key arguments that are likely to co-occur in text.

Sentences that contain the chosen key arguments are candidate event mentions; verbs appearing frequently in such sentences that are discriminative across event types are likely triggers → define Trigger Candidate Frequency (TCF) and Trigger Event Type Frequency (TETF) → TR ranks verbs.

Initial verbal trigger lexicon from TR is noisy and misses nominal triggers → map Freebase event types to FrameNet frames using averaged word embeddings of type names and LUs → filter verbal triggers outside mapped frames and add nominal lexical units from mapped frames.
Soft Distant Supervision (SDS): label sentences that contain all key arguments and a mapped trigger as positive examples for that event and assign argument roles from detected mentions.

Train event extraction models on the generated data (with DMCNN + MIL to mitigate noise). Evaluate (manual precision, held-out against Freebase, and extrinsic performance on ACE) → claim: dataset has high manual precision and utility to augment ACE training, and MIL helps mitigate noise.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes an end-to-end pipeline to automatically generate large-scale event extraction training data by combining world knowledge (Freebase CVTs) and linguistic knowledge (FrameNet). It ranks event arguments using a Key Rate (KR = Role Saliency * Event Relevance) computed from Freebase counts to select a small set of 'key arguments' per CVT; it then finds trigger candidate verbs via a Trigger Rate (TR = TCF * TETF) measured from sentences that mention those key arguments; FrameNet is mapped to Freebase event types via averaged word embeddings to filter noisy verb triggers and add nominal triggers; finally a Soft Distant Supervision (SDS) rule labels sentences that contain all chosen key arguments plus a mapped trigger as expressing the event and assigns argument roles accordingly. The authors release two datasets (KA-only: ~421k sentences; KA+T: ~72k sentences), report manual precision estimates from a 500-sample annotation (trigger ~88.9%, argument ~85.4%), and demonstrate extrinsic utility by training DMCNNs with multi-instance learning (DMCNN-MIL): ED-only is competitive with ACE-trained models and ACE+ED improves ACE baselines. Ablations compare KR vs RS/ER and TR with FrameNet vs variants. The paper chains these components into a practical, reproducible pipeline but relies on several heuristics (embedding-average mapping, substring/NER matching, thresholded KR/TR), manual mappings (to ACE types), and validation limited by a modest manual sample and held-out evaluation against an incomplete KB (Freebase). I reconstruct the argument as: (1) Freebase provides abundant structured event instances but lacks triggers; (2) selecting a small set of discriminative, mentionable arguments (KR) lets one find candidate sentences in text; (3) verbs in those sentences with high TR are likely triggers; (4) FrameNet mapping can filter/expand triggers including nominals; (5) SDS (key args + trigger => event) yields largely correct labels; (6) noisy labels can be mitigated with MIL during model training, producing useful extractors and augmenting ACE.

Key arguments + Wikipedia (NER/matching) -> find sentences containing key arguments -> collect candidate verbs
Candidate verbs statistics (TCF, TETF) -> compute TR -> initial verbal trigger lexicon
Freebase event type name embeddings vs FrameNet LU embeddings -> choose mapped frame -> filter TR verbs not in frame and add nouns from frame -> expanded trigger lexicon
SDS rule: sentence containing all key arguments + trigger -> label event type, trigger, argument roles

Assembled labeled dataset (KA-only; KA+T) -> train DMCNNs with MIL -> evaluate held-out (Freebase) and manual samples -> extrinsic test on ACE (with manual mapping) shows improvement when combining ACE+ED
Ablation: KR vs RS/ER and TR vs TCF/TETF and FrameNet show modest but consistent gains; MIL reduces DS noise

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a multi-stage Soft Distant Supervision (SDS) pipeline that (1) selects a small set of "key arguments" per Freebase CVT via a Key Rate (KR = Role Saliency * Event Relevance), (2) finds trigger-candidate verbs from Wikipedia sentences containing those key arguments using Trigger Rate (TR = TCF * TETF), (3) maps Freebase event-type names to FrameNet frames using averaged word embeddings to filter verbal triggers and add nominal triggers, and (4) labels sentences as event mentions if they contain all chosen key arguments plus a mapped trigger (SDS). The authors release automatically labeled datasets (421k KA-only; 72.6k KA+T) for 21 Freebase event types, report manual precision estimates on a 500-sample annotation (trigger ~88.9%, argument ~85.4%), and show extrinsic improvements when augmenting ACE training data (ACE+ED) and competitive performance when training on ED-only. Ablations indicate KR outperforms RS/ER and TR + FrameNet outperforms simple TR/TCF/TETF variants. A DMCNN with MIL is used to mitigate label noise and is shown to help in held-out and manual evaluations. Evidence from manuscript sections, tables, and figures supports most factual claims about dataset sizes, pipeline architecture, and evaluation set-ups. Primary uncertainties arise from heuristic choices (embedding averaging for mapping), annotation procedure (annotators include an author, single 500-sample pool), manual Freebase→ACE mapping, limited per-event-type statistics and lack of statistical testing, and evaluation sensitivity to KB incompleteness and hyperparameters.

Find Wikipedia sentences containing all chosen key arguments -> use verb frequency in those sentences to compute TCF and TETF -> TR = TCF * TETF ranks verbal trigger candidates.
Map Freebase event type names to FrameNet frames via averaged word embeddings -> use mapped frames to filter noisy verbs and add nominal triggers.
Apply Soft Distant Supervision: sentence with key arguments + mapped trigger -> label sentence with event type and argument roles.
Train DMCNN with MIL on resulting noisy labeled data -> MIL mitigates noise and yields extractors that are competitive with ACE-trained models; augmenting ACE with ED improves ACE performance.

evidence: Figure 4 and §3 describe the four components (Key argument detection, Trigger detection, Trigger filtering/expansion, SDS labeling).
§3.1-3.4 provide formal definitions for KR, TR, FrameNet mapping (Eqns 1-7) and SDS assumption statements.
uncertainty_flags: Individual component effectiveness depends on heuristic formulas and hyperparameters; ablations shown are helpful but limited to selected 21 event types.
FrameNet mapping via averaged embeddings is heuristic and mapping accuracy is not quantified; may fail for multi-word or ambiguous Freebase names.

identified_claims.claim_text: The automatically generated dataset contains 421,602 sentences labeled using key-arguments-only and 72,611 sentences labeled using key-arguments plus triggers, covering 21 selected Freebase CVT event types (sum of ~3.87M Freebase instances).
evidence: Table 2 shows totals: 3,870,492 Freebase instances, 421,602 KA sentences, 72,611 KA+T sentences for 21 events.
§5.1 notes hyperparameters K=2 and TR threshold=0.8 used to produce these counts.
uncertainty_flags: Counts are sensitive to hyperparameter settings (K, TR) chosen by grid search; other settings yield different scales.
Coverage limited to 21 manually selected CVTs; not representative of all Freebase CVTs.

identified_claims.claim_text: Manual inspection on a random sample (500 samples, 3 annotators majority vote, inter-annotator agreement 87.5%) yields average precision ~88.9% for trigger labeling and ~85.4% for argument labeling on the final 72,611 labeled sentences.
evidence: §5.2 describes the annotation protocol: 500 random samples, 3 annotators (one author + two colleagues), majority vote; inter-agreement reported as 87.5%.
Table 3 reports trigger labeling precision 88.9% and argument labeling precision 85.4% (stage averages).
uncertainty_flags: Sample size (500) relative to dataset (72k) is modest; no confidence intervals or variance reported.
Annotators include an author and colleagues—possible bias or lack of blind external validation.
No per-event-type precision reported; aggregate average may mask type-specific failure modes.

identified_claims.claim_text: Models trained on the automatically labeled data perform competitively with models trained on human-annotated ACE data, and combining automatic data with ACE training data improves event extraction performance on ACE test sets.
evidence: Table 4: DMCNN trained on ACE+ED achieves higher overall F1 than DMCNN trained on ACE only for both trigger and argument tasks.
Text: "DMCNN trained with ACE+ED achieves the highest performance... DMCNN trained with ED Only achieves a competitive performance."
uncertainty_flags: Manual mapping between Freebase event types and ACE event types is used but mapping details are not provided — may affect fairness.
No statistical significance testing reported; improvements are moderate (~1-2 F1 points in some measures).
Potential for document overlap / leakage (Wikipedia-based labeling vs ACE test documents) not explicitly ruled out.

identified_claims.claim_text: Proposed ranking metrics (Key Rate KR for arguments and Trigger Rate TR for verbs) and the use of FrameNet for trigger filtering/expansion are effective components in producing useful labels.
evidence: Table 5: ACE+KR yields higher Trigger F1 (70.5) and Argument F1 (55.7) than ACE+RS and ACE+ER.
Table 6: ACE+TR+FrameNet yields Trigger F1 70.5 and Argument F1 55.7, higher than ACE+TCF/TETF/TR alone.
uncertainty_flags: Improvements are modest and per-metric; no p-values or confidence intervals shown.
KR and TR depend on counts from Freebase/Wikipedia; sensitivity to KB sparsity not fully studied.
FrameNet mapping is heuristic (averaged embeddings) and mapping accuracy is unreported.

identified_claims.claim_text: Using Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) with DMCNNs (DMCNNs-MIL) is effective at mitigating noise from distant supervision in both held-out and manual evaluations for event extraction.
evidence: §4 describes DMCNN-MIL architecture and objective (Eqns 8-10).
§5.5 contains held-out P-R curves (Figures 7-8) showing MIL variants outperforming non-MIL variants and mentions manual top-n evaluation where DMCNNs-MIL achieved best performance.
uncertainty_flags: Held-out evaluation uses Freebase as silver standard and thus can undercount true positives (KB incompleteness); precision-recall curves may be biased.
Details and numerical values for the manual top-n evaluation (Table 7) are not fully reproduced in the manuscript excerpt; sample sizes and significance unknown.
Comparative baselines, hyperparameters, and training details for MIL vs non-MIL variants are not exhaustively specified.

strengths.title: Coherent multi-component pipeline
strengths.description: The paper lays out a clear sequence of algorithmic steps (KR, TR, FrameNet mapping, SDS, MIL training) with formal definitions and an ablation-friendly design.
evidence: Figure 4 and §3 describe the pipeline architecture; Eqns 1-7 define KR/TR and mapping.

strengths.title: Large-scale released resource
strengths.description: The authors release a sizable automatically labeled dataset (421k KA-only; 72k KA+T) that can be useful for follow-up research.
evidence: §5.1 and Table 2 report dataset sizes and provide a download link in §2/Intro.

strengths.title: Empirical ablations and extrinsic validation
strengths.description: The manuscript includes ablations (KR vs RS/ER; TR vs TCF/TETF; effect of FrameNet) and extrinsic ACE experiments showing practical utility of the generated data.
evidence: Tables 4-6 and §5.3-5.4 present these comparisons and results.

concerns.title: Manual evaluation sampling and annotator bias
concerns.description: Manual precision is estimated on 500 random samples annotated by three annotators including an author and two colleagues; this small, non-independent pool and lack of stratified sampling limit generalizability and risk optimistic precision estimates.
evidence: §5.2: "500 randomly selected samples... three annotators (including one of the authors and two colleagues) ... inter-agreement 87.5%"; Table 3 reports precision values.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-run manual annotation with an independent, blinded annotator pool; stratify sampling by event type and by KA-only vs KA+T; report per-type precision, confidence intervals, and inter-annotator agreement excluding authors.

concerns.title: Underspecified and heuristic FrameNet mapping
concerns.description: Mapping Freebase event-type names to FrameNet frames by averaging embeddings of type-name words is heuristic. The paper lacks quantitative validation of mapping correctness and failure modes; wrong mappings could both remove valid triggers and add irrelevant nominal triggers.
evidence: §3.3 describes frame(i) = argmax_j similarity(ei, ej,k) using average word embeddings (Eq.7); §5.4 claims benefit but mapping accuracy is not measured.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a quantitative evaluation of the mapping on a held-out sample: annotate correct/incorrect mappings, report precision/recall of mapped frames, and include qualitative error analysis; consider alternative mapping methods (e.g., supervised classifier, lexical matching, or contextualized embeddings) and compare.

concerns.title: Manual Freebase→ACE type mapping and potential evaluation leakage
concerns.description: Extrinsic ACE experiments rely on a manual mapping from Freebase CVT types to ACE event types, but this mapping is not documented; additionally, potential overlap between Wikipedia (used to label ED) and ACE test documents is not ruled out, risking evaluation leakage.
evidence: §5.3: "We mapped these types of events manually and we add them into ACE training corpus." No mapping table is provided; §5.1 uses Wikipedia snapshot (Jan 2016).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Publish the explicit Freebase→ACE mapping table; verify and report that ACE test documents are disjoint from the Wikipedia documents used during labeling, or remove overlapping documents and re-run ACE experiments; report per-type results and significance tests.

concerns.title: Sensitivity to hyperparameters and selection of 21 event types
concerns.description: Key hyperparameters (K=2, TR=0.8) and the choice of 21 CVTs are determined by grid search and manual filtering, but the paper lacks sensitivity analyses and justification for generalizability beyond selected types.
evidence: §5.1 notes "Two hyper parameters... are set as 2 and 0.8, by grid search respectively." §2 mentions selection of 21 CVTs after filtering.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide sensitivity plots showing dataset sizes and downstream performance across a range of K and TR values; report how many CVTs were filtered out and why; include experiments on additional CVTs or a randomized subset to assess generalizability.

concerns.title: Held-out evaluation relies on incomplete KB and lacks reconciliation with manual checks
concerns.description: Held-out evaluation compares model predictions to held-out Freebase entries, but Freebase incompleteness causes false negatives. Although a manual top-n evaluation is reported, the paper does not reconcile held-out and manual evaluations quantitatively or report error rates for Freebase false negatives.
evidence: §5.5 describes held-out evaluation and notes Freebase incompleteness; manual top-n evaluation is described but detailed numbers and reconciliation are limited.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Estimate the Freebase false-negative rate by manually checking a random subset of model 'false positives' from held-out evaluation; report adjusted precision/recall or provide qualitative analysis of common cases.

concerns.title: Entity mention/linking heuristics under-described
concerns.description: The process of identifying that a Wikipedia sentence 'contains all key arguments' relies on CoreNLP NER and string matching, but alias handling, coreference, and ambiguous names are not discussed; matching reliability may strongly affect label recall and precision.
evidence: §3.2: use of Stanford CoreNLP for sentence segmentation, POS, NER; selection of sentences that 'contain all key arguments' is described but matching procedures (aliases, coref) are not detailed.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Describe exact matching heuristics and entity normalization steps. Report recall of argument mention detection by annotating a sample of instances and measuring how often Freebase argument values are found in the same sentence using the implemented heuristics; consider using entity linking or alias dictionaries to improve recall.

concerns.title: Lack of statistical testing and per-type breakdowns
concerns.description: Reported improvements (e.g., ACE+ED over ACE) are modest and not accompanied by statistical significance tests or per-event-type performance breakdowns.
evidence: Tables 4-6 show F1 improvements but no p-values, CIs, or per-type breakdowns are provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report statistical significance (e.g., bootstrap or paired test) for primary comparisons and include per-event-type P/R/F to reveal whether gains are concentrated in certain types.

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational distant supervision for relation extraction; motivates using KBs to label text for supervised learning without manual labels.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar in spirit (automatic supervision from KB), but Mintz focuses on static relations (entity pairs) whereas current paper adapts and extends DS ideas to complex events, adding KR/TR heuristics and FrameNet.

comparable_works.relevance: Applied DS to a specific event type (plane crash slot filling).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Shows prior attempts to extend DS to events but limited to single event type with strong constraints; current paper aims at many event types and proposes general heuristics.

comparable_works.relevance: CNN architecture used as supervised baseline and as the modeling backbone with MIL in this paper.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Same DMCNN base model; this paper uses DMCNN with MIL trained on automatically labeled data and compares to Chen et al.'s ACE-trained DMCNN.

comparable_works.citation_label: Hoffmann et al. 2011; Surdeanu et al. 2012
comparable_works.relevance: Work on multi-instance and noisy supervision for relation extraction; motivates use of MIL to mitigate DS noise.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides DS noise mitigation foundations; current paper applies MIL to event-extraction setting originating from more complex KB-to-text matching.

comparable_works.relevance: Unsupervised event extraction by clustering parallel news streams to create training data; retrieved literature indicates other unsupervised approaches to generate event training data.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Alternative approach generating sentence clusters as training data; differs in using parallel streams and clustering versus Freebase + FrameNet heuristics.

uncertainty_flags: FrameNet mapping via averaged embeddings is heuristic and its accuracy is unquantified.
Manual precision estimates come from a 500-sample annotation with annotators including an author; possible bias and lack of stratification.
Freebase→ACE mapping for extrinsic evaluation is manual and undocumented; potential mapping bias.
Dataset construction choices (21 selected CVTs; K and TR hyperparameters) limit generalizability.
Held-out evaluation uses Freebase as silver standard and may undercount true positives due to KB incompleteness.
alternative_interpretations: Observed ACE improvements from augmenting ACE with ED may partially reflect favorable manual mapping choices and overlaps in domain rather than broad utility; careful mapping and leakage checks could reduce the observed gains.

High aggregate manual precision may be driven by a subset of event types (e.g., marriage) where arguments and triggers are explicit; other event types may have substantially lower precision that are hidden in averages.
FrameNet-based trigger expansion benefits may come primarily from a few high-frequency nominal triggers; for rarer or more ambiguous event types, the mapping could hurt by adding noise.
transparency_notes: The manuscript omits the explicit Freebase→ACE mapping table and exact preprocessing scripts for entity matching; these are necessary for reproducibility and should be released with the dataset and code.
Hyperparameter selection logs (grid search results) and random seeds are not provided; reporting them would improve reproducibility of dataset sizes and thresholds.
Manual annotation guidelines and anonymized annotator IDs (to confirm independence) should be published for the 500-sample evaluation.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The pipeline combines known elements (distant supervision, MIL, FrameNet, word embeddings) in a novel assembly for event extraction; lack of close precedent does not imply correctness—robust measurement of heuristic steps and mapping quality is needed to establish validity.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If Freebase CVT argument fields are frequently mentioned together in the same Wikipedia sentence (or can be reliably linked), KR+SDS will produce high-precision labels and the approach succeeds.

If averaged word embeddings reliably map Freebase type names to appropriate FrameNet frames for a substantial fraction of event types, FrameNet filtering/expansion will reduce noise and increase nominal trigger coverage.

If entity matching (NER/string matching) recovers argument mentions with high recall and precision (including aliases), the pipeline will yield useful coverage; poor matching would drastically reduce recall and introduce ambiguity.
If MIL effectively selects correct instance-level signals in bags despite systematic biases in SDS labeling, models trained on ED will generalize and augment human data.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Combines multiple established components (KB distant supervision, embedding-based mapping, FrameNet, MIL, CNN models) into an end-to-end pipeline and produces a sizable released dataset; the idea is pragmatic rather than theoretically novel.
evidence: Use of KR/TR heuristics, FrameNet mapping, and DMCNN-MIL applied to event extraction; ablations show modest gains.
uncertainty_flags: Effectiveness may be dataset- and selection-dependent; mapping heuristics unvalidated.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The 72k/421k labeled sentences across 21 event types represent a practical contribution for the community, enabling research on noisy supervision and large-scale event extraction.
evidence: Table 2 dataset sizes and claim of release via GitHub.
uncertainty_flags: Quality and per-type reliability need more transparent validation (per-type precision, reproducible scripts).

confidence_interval.rationale: High confidence that the manuscript correctly documents the described pipeline, dataset sizes, and evaluations (supported by explicit sections/tables). Moderate-to-high uncertainty remains about generalizability, mapping accuracy (FrameNet), annotator bias in manual evaluation, and sensitivity to hyperparameters—these warrant the recommended reproducibility and additional analyses.

consensus_findings: The paper presents a coherent, modular pipeline combining Freebase CVTs (KB), Key Rate (KR) for key-argument selection, Trigger Rate (TR) for verb ranking, embedding-based mapping to FrameNet for trigger filtering/expansion, and a Soft Distant Supervision (SDS) rule to generate large-scale event-extraction training data.

A released resource was produced: approximately 421,602 sentences labeled using key-arguments-only (KA) and 72,611 sentences labeled using key-arguments plus triggers (KA+T) across 21 selected Freebase CVT event types.

Intrinsic (manual sampling) and extrinsic (training DMCNN variants including MIL and testing on ACE) evaluations were performed; aggregate manual precision reported is high (trigger labeling ~88.9%, argument labeling ~85.4%), and augmenting ACE with the automatic data (ACE+ED) yields modest downstream F1 improvements.

Ablation experiments indicate KR (vs RS/ER), TR variants, and FrameNet-based trigger expansion produce small but consistent performance gains in the evaluated ACE setting, and multi-instance learning (MIL) aids robustness to distant-supervision noise.
disagreements: Magnitude and generality of gains: reviewers differ on whether ACE improvements and ablation gains demonstrate broad utility (some see practical significance; others view gains as modest and possibly dependent on mapping choices or dataset selection).

Novelty assessment: some reviewers view the combined pipeline and released dataset as a valuable engineering/resource contribution and an interesting operational idea (KR + FrameNet), while others regard the work as incremental relative to prior distant-supervision and MIL literature.

Adequacy of manual evaluation: reviewers agree manual checks were done but disagree about whether a single 500-sample annotation with annotators including an author is sufficient without stratification and external annotators.

Reliability of embedding-based FrameNet mapping: reviewers accept empirical benefits reported but disagree about whether the paper validates the mapping heuristic sufficiently to claim general reliability.
uncertainty_hotspots: FrameNet mapping accuracy: mapping Freebase type names to FrameNet frames via averaged word embeddings is heuristic; per-type mapping precision, recall, and failure modes are not reported.

Manual annotation representativeness: the 500-sample manual evaluation used annotators including an author, lacked stratification by event type, and reported no confidence intervals or per-type breakdowns.

Freebase->ACE mapping and potential leakage: the manual mapping used for extrinsic ACE evaluation is not published in the paper excerpt, and document overlap between Wikipedia-derived labeled sentences and ACE test documents is not explicitly ruled out.

Entity mention/linking reliability: matching Freebase argument values to Wikipedia sentences uses CoreNLP NER and string matching, but alias handling, coreference, and matching recall/precision are unspecified.

Hyperparameter sensitivity and CVT selection: dataset size/quality depend on chosen K (number of key arguments), TR threshold, and the hand-selected 21 CVTs; robustness across these choices is incompletely reported.
Held-out evaluation validity: held-out evaluation uses Freebase as a silver standard (an incomplete KB), so P/R curves may be biased by false negatives; reconciliation with manual checks is limited.
model_diversity_effects: Component-level effects: ablations isolating KR vs RS/ER and TR variants (with/without FrameNet) show that heuristic choices materially affect downstream ACE performance, indicating modular design enables measurable component contributions.

Training paradigm effects: using MIL (bag-level supervision) changes training dynamics with noisy SDS labels and yields better held-out/manual precision compared to instance-level training, demonstrating model-level robustness differences.

Resource/version dependence: outcomes depend on external artifacts (Freebase snapshot, FrameNet coverage, pre-trained embeddings, CoreNLP behavior); changing these resources or their versions could substantially alter results.

Volume vs. method tension: reviewers differ on whether observed improvements stem primarily from increased training volume (ED augmenting ACE) or from the specific KR/TR/FrameNet heuristics; this interpretive variance reflects model/data coupling sensitivity.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the submission as an engineering/resource contribution that demonstrates a plausible pipeline for large-scale weakly supervised event-labeling but requires additional transparency and validation before strong claims of generality. Request artifacts and analyses prioritized as follows: (1) publish mapping tables (Freebase CVT -> FrameNet frames with similarity scores/top-k candidates; Freebase CVT -> ACE event types) and the selection list of 21 CVTs with filtering criteria; (2) release preprocessing and entity-matching code (string-normalization rules, alias lists, entity-linking or coreference steps) and describe NER settings; (3) verify and report any overlap between Wikipedia pages used for labeling and ACE dev/test documents and, if overlap exists, provide extrinsic evaluations excluding overlapping documents; (4) extend manual evaluation with independent, blinded annotators using stratified sampling across event types (report per-type precision/recall with 95% confidence intervals and an error taxonomy for SDS failures); (5) provide a quantitative audit of Freebase->FrameNet mappings (manual spot-checks, mapping precision/recall) and consider alternative mapping strategies or confidence thresholds; (6) present sensitivity analyses showing dataset size and downstream performance as functions of K and TR thresholds and include grid-search logs and validation criteria; (7) release full model/training hyperparameters, random seeds, bag-construction scripts, and, if possible, trained checkpoints. Emphasize that the editor should weigh these reproducibility and robustness items when integrating reviewer perspectives—current disagreement centers on generality and validation rather than whether the pipeline was implemented and evaluated as described.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen reproducibility and support claims, provide the following along with the dataset/code release: (1) explicit mapping tables: Freebase CVT -> FrameNet frame (include similarity scores and top-k candidates) and Freebase CVT -> ACE type mapping with annotation notes for ambiguous cases; (2) preprocessing and matching code: exact NER settings, string normalization, alias/redirect handling, any coreference or entity-linking steps, and scripts used to select sentences containing key arguments; (3) hyperparameter logs and sensitivity plots showing dataset size and downstream ACE performance across K and TR values and justification for chosen operating points; (4) expanded manual evaluation: annotate a larger, stratified sample using independent, blinded annotators, report per-type precision/recall with 95% CIs, inter-annotator agreement excluding authors, and an error taxonomy (incidental mentions, cross-sentence argument mentions, incorrect triggers, mapping errors); (5) FrameNet mapping audit: manual validation of a representative sample of mappings, report mapping precision/recall and failure examples, and optionally compare to alternative mapping methods (contextual embeddings or supervised classifiers); (6) leakage check: demonstrate document-level disjointness between Wikipedia used for labeling and ACE dev/test or provide rerun results excluding overlaps; (7) MIL/model reproducibility: list full model and training hyperparameters, random seeds, bag construction heuristics, and release training/evaluation scripts and trained checkpoints to enable replication. Where results depend on heuristics or manual mappings, temper claims to reflect conditional validity and include statistical significance testing for primary comparisons.
transparency_report: Formal definitions and equations: KR and TR formulas (Equations 1-6), embedding-based mapping equation (Eq.7), and SDS labeling rule are present in the manuscript.
Dataset summaries and release: Table 2 reports dataset sizes (3,870,492 Freebase instances; 421,602 KA sentences; 72,611 KA+T sentences) and a GitHub release is indicated.

Manual-evaluation protocol and aggregate metrics: a 500-sample manual annotation with 3 annotators (one author + two colleagues) and aggregate trigger/argument precision values (~88.9% and ~85.4%) are reported (Table 3).
Ablations and extrinsic results: Tables 4-6 present ACE extrinsic comparisons and component ablations; DMCNN-MIL held-out and manual evaluations are referenced (Figures 7-8, Table 7).

Missing artifacts requested for reproducibility: Freebase CVT -> ACE mapping table; Freebase CVT -> FrameNet mapping table and confidence scores; complete preprocessing and entity-matching scripts (alias handling, normalization, coreference/linking); grid-search logs and validation criteria for K/TR hyperparameters; per-event-type labeled-instance counts and per-type manual-precision breakdowns; full numeric values for held-out/manual evaluations and statistical significance testing; complete DMCNN-MIL training hyperparameters and random seeds.
epistemic_limits: This synthesis is limited to the provided paper excerpts and reviewer summaries. Key empirical uncertainties remain because certain artifacts (mapping tables, preprocessing code, hyperparameter logs) and expanded evaluations (stratified/independent manual annotation, per-type metrics, leakage checks) were not available for independent verification. Consequently, conclusions about generalizability beyond the 21 selected CVTs, the absolute dataset quality across the long tail of event types, and the robustness of embedding-based FrameNet mapping are provisional. Independent reproduction using the requested artifacts and expanded analyses is necessary to reduce these epistemic uncertainties.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript describes an end-to-end pipeline to automatically generate large-scale event-extraction training data by combining Freebase CVT instances (world knowledge) and FrameNet (linguistic knowledge) under a Soft Distant Supervision (SDS) labeling rule. Key algorithmic pieces are Key Rate (KR) for selecting top-K key arguments from KB counts, Trigger Rate (TR) for ranking candidate verbs, and an embedding-averaging mapping from Freebase type names to FrameNet frames to filter/expand triggers. The authors release two datasets (≈421k sentences using key-arguments-only; ≈72.6k sentences including triggers for 21 selected CVTs), provide a 500-sample manual precision check (reported trigger precision ≈88.9%, argument precision ≈85.4%), ablation studies (KR vs RS/ER; TR with/without FrameNet), held-out evaluations against Freebase, and extrinsic tests where models trained on the generated data (with DMCNN and DMCNN-MIL) are combined with ACE training data and report modest improvements on ACE test sets.
strengths: Coherent, modular pipeline linking KB-derived argument ranking (KR), trigger discovery (TR), FrameNet-driven filtering/expansion, and SDS labeling (paper: §3, Figure 4; Equations 1–7).
A sizable released resource: reported totals of ≈3.87M Freebase instances producing ≈421,602 KA sentences and ≈72,611 KA+T sentences for 21 CVTs (Table 2; §5.1).

Practical extrinsic evaluation: training standard extraction models (DMCNN, DMCNN-MIL) on generated labels and showing that ACE+ED improves ACE performance (Table 4; §5.3), plus ablations to tie component choices to downstream effects (Tables 5–6).
Application of MIL to mitigate distant-supervision noise and report of held-out P–R curves and manual top-n checks indicating MIL helps (§4, §5.5; Figures 7–8).
limitations: Manual-evaluation design is limited: precision estimates derive from a 500-sample annotation by three annotators including an author and two colleagues with no stratification by event type and no reported confidence intervals—this raises risks of optimistic bias and poor representativeness (§5.2; Table 3).

Key mapping and preprocessing artifacts are underspecified: the Freebase CVT -> ACE mapping used for ACE extrinsic evaluation is not published in the manuscript, the Freebase -> FrameNet mapping (Eq.7) is a heuristic (averaged embeddings) with no quantitative audit, and entity-linking/matching heuristics (string normalization, alias handling, coreference) used to detect argument mentions in Wikipedia are not detailed (§3.3, §3.2, §5.3).

Held-out evaluation depends on Freebase as silver-standard: Freebase incompleteness introduces false negatives in held-out P–R measurements and the manuscript provides only limited manual reconciliation (top-n) without estimating overall false-negative rates (§5.5).

Sensitivity and generalizability are underreported: dataset scale and quality depend on hyperparameters (K, TR threshold) and on the manual selection of 21 CVTs; sensitivity curves, grid-search logs, per-CVT performance, and behavior on additional CVTs are not fully reported (§5.1, §5.4).
open_questions: Please provide the explicit Freebase CVT -> ACE mapping table used in extrinsic experiments and report per-ACE-type counts and per-type P/R/F when ACE is trained with and without ED. Were any mapping decisions ambiguous and how were they resolved? (§5.3 referenced but mapping not shown).

Can the authors release the Freebase CVT -> FrameNet mapping (top-k candidate frames and similarity scores from Eq.7) and a manual audit (precision/recall) of those mappings on a representative sample of CVTs? How sensitive are downstream gains to incorrect mappings? (§3.3, §5.4).

Provide details and evaluation of the entity matching process used to decide that a Wikipedia sentence 'contains all key arguments': exact NER configuration, string-normalization/alias rules, whether entity linking or coreference was used, and an estimate of matching precision/recall measured on an annotated sample (§3.2).

Report sensitivity analyses: dataset size and downstream ACE performance across K (number of key arguments) and TR thresholds, grid-search validation criterion and logs, and whether ACE test documents overlap with Wikipedia pages used for labeling (leakage check). If overlap exists, provide rerun results excluding overlaps (§5.1, §5.4, shared analysis notes).
consensus_snapshot: All reviewers reconstruct the pipeline and agree the authors implemented and evaluated it: KR/TR/FrameNet/SDS pipeline, datasets released (421k KA; 72k KA+T), manual sampling, ablations, held-out and ACE extrinsic evaluations (see §3, §5, Tables 2–6).

There is agreement that MIL is an appropriate and effective approach to mitigate distant-supervision noise in this setting and that ablations indicate KR and FrameNet components produced small but consistent gains on ACE in reported experiments.
Reviewers concur that the work is primarily an engineering/resource contribution: an assembly of established techniques with pragmatic heuristics producing a useful released dataset.
disagreement_snapshot: Interpretation of effect size: some reviewers view the ACE improvements and ablation gains as practically meaningful and indicative of pipeline utility, while others consider the gains modest, possibly attributable to increased training volume or to favorable manual mappings rather than robust methodological superiority.

Novelty characterization: several reviewers emphasize practical novelty in assembling components and releasing a dataset, while others emphasize that the methodological elements (DS, MIL, FrameNet, CNNs) are incremental and that the new heuristics (KR/TR, embedding-based mapping) require stronger validation.

Sufficiency of current validation: some reviewers feel current manual checks and ablations are adequate to show promise, whereas others demand larger, stratified external annotation, mapping audits, leakage checks, and sensitivity analyses before generality claims are supported.
uncertainty_snapshot: FrameNet mapping fidelity: uncertainty about how often the embedding-averaging mapping (Eq.7) yields correct frame alignments and how incorrect mappings affect trigger lexicons and label quality.

Manual-precision generalizability: uncertainty that the reported ≈88.9% trigger and ≈85.4% argument precision (500-sample, mixed annotator pool) reflect whole-dataset quality—per-type heterogeneity or annotator bias could alter these estimates substantially.
Held-out evaluation bias: Freebase incompleteness leads to unknown false-negative rates in held-out P–R; the direction and magnitude of this bias are not quantified.
Hyperparameter and selection sensitivity: unknown robustness when varying K, TR, and when applying pipeline to CVTs beyond the 21 selected types; current results may be contingent on these choices.

Related literature: Reschke et al., 2014 (DS for event-slot filling) and Zhang et al. (News-Spike/parallel-news unsupervised event data generation) referenced as closest prior efforts to automatic event-data creation (specialist reviews).
transparency_notes: Key formal definitions, pipeline steps, dataset totals, ablation tables, and the reported manual-evaluation protocol are present in the manuscript (Equations 1–7; Figure 4; Tables 2–6; §5.2). Missing or incompletely reported artifacts that limit reproducibility and confidence include: (1) the explicit Freebase CVT -> ACE mapping table used for ACE experiments and per-type counts; (2) the Freebase CVT -> FrameNet mapping outputs (top-k frames and similarity scores) and a manual audit of mapping correctness; (3) preprocessing and entity-matching code (NER settings, string normalization rules, alias handling, coreference/entity-linking heuristics) used to detect argument mentions in Wikipedia; (4) grid-search logs, validation criteria, and sensitivity curves for K and TR hyperparameters; (5) per-event-type labeled-instance counts and per-type manual-precision breakdowns with confidence intervals; (6) full model/training hyperparameters, random seeds, bag construction scripts for MIL, and numeric values for held-out/manual evaluations including sample sizes. human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Consider the submission as a practical engineering/resource contribution that demonstrates a plausible pipeline with a released dataset and initial evaluations; however, prioritize requests for additional transparency and validation before treating generality claims as established. Strengths: coherent modular design with formalized heuristics (Equations 1–7; Figure 4), a substantial released dataset (Table 2), ablations linking design choices to downstream gains (Tables 5–6), and application of MIL to mitigate DS noise (§4, §5.5). Limitations: (1) Manual precision is estimated from 500 samples annotated by a small, non-independent annotator pool (includes an author), without stratified per-type breakdowns or confidence intervals—this threatens representativeness and may bias precision estimates (§5.2; Table 3). Additional concerns: held-out evaluation uses Freebase as silver-standard without quantifying false negatives (§5.5), and sensitivity to hyperparameters (K, TR) and to the 21 CVT selection is underreported (§5.1, §5.4). Open Questions: (1) Please release the Freebase->ACE mapping and per-ACE-type results with counts and statistical tests. (2) Please publish the Freebase->FrameNet mapping outputs and a manual audit (precision/recall) of mappings—how often are mappings correct and how do mapping errors affect trigger lexicon quality? (4) Share sensitivity analyses (dataset size and downstream F1 versus K and TR), grid-search logs, and a leakage check for overlaps between Wikipedia and ACE test/dev. Weld Computer Science & Engineering University of Washington Seattle, W A 98195, USA {clzhang, soderlan, weld }@cs.washington.edu Abstract Most approaches to relation extraction , the task of extracting ground facts from natural language text, are based on machine learning and thus starved by scarce training data. Man- ual annotation is too expensive to scale to a comprehensive set of relations. Distant super- vision, which automatically creates training data, only works with relations that already populate a knowledge base (KB). Unfortu- nately, KBs such as FreeBase rarely cover event relations ( e.g. “person travels to loca- tion”). Thus, the problem of extracting a wide range of events — e.g., from news streams — is an important, open challenge. This paper introduces N EWS SPIKE -RE, a novel, unsupervised algorithm that discovers event relations and then learns to extract them. NEWS SPIKE -RE uses a novel probabilistic graphical model to cluster sentences describ- ing similar events from parallel news streams. These clusters then comprise training data for the extractor. Our evaluation shows that NEWS SPIKE -RE generates high quality train- ing sentences and learns extractors that per- form much better than rival approaches, more than doubling the area under a precision-recall curve compared to Universal Schemas. 1

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Weld Computer Science & Engineering University of Washington Seattle, W A 98195, USA {clzhang, soderlan, weld }@cs.washington.edu Abstract Most approaches to relation extraction , the task of extracting ground facts from natural language text, are based on machine learning and thus starved by scarce training data. Man- ual annotation is too expensive to scale to a comprehensive set of relations. Distant super- vision, which automatically creates training data, only works with relations that already populate a knowledge base (KB). Unfortu- nately, KBs such as FreeBase rarely cover event relations ( e.g. “person travels to loca- tion”). Thus, the problem of extracting a wide range of events — e.g., from news streams — is an important, open challenge. This paper introduces N EWS SPIKE -RE, a novel, unsupervised algorithm that discovers event relations and then learns to extract them. NEWS SPIKE -RE uses a novel probabilistic graphical model to cluster sentences describ- ing similar events from parallel news streams. These clusters then comprise training data for the extractor. Our evaluation shows that NEWS SPIKE -RE generates high quality train- ing sentences and learns extractors that per- form much better than rival approaches, more than doubling the area under a precision-recall curve compared to Universal Schemas. 1

These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
